1.why: Validation compares the submitted token strictly against the server-side session's stored resetToken, which is only set when the request was for the known mock account, binding the code to that user/session.

2.why: A code is only accepted if it equals session.resetToken of the issuing session, so the same code fails for any other session/user.

3.why: Password update only clears the reset token fields; the session itself is never invalidated and continues on to MFA and authenticated state, and no cross-session invalidation exists.

4.why: HTTPS is enforced with TLS certs, HSTS, and an HTTP rejection port, but no TLS version is configured in the code, so 'latest TLS version' cannot be confirmed.

5.why: Passwords are bcrypt-hashed at cost 12, but reset tokens are stored in plaintext session memory and the MFA code is a hardcoded plaintext constant.

6.why: No actual email is sent — delivery is simulated locally in the browser — and the simulated message contains only the reset code, no other private user data.

7.why: The server validates email, token, and password formats, and the client builds all UI via createElement/textContent so user input is never rendered as HTML.

8.why: The application performs no redirects at all; navigation is internal screen state and origin validation restricts requests to https://localhost:3000.

9.why: There are no email templates; the simulated delivery message is system-generated plain text inserted via textContent, with CSP nonces blocking any injected scripts.

10.why: The reset code and MFA code are deliberately written into the on-page log panel and via console.log, so tokens do appear in logs despite generic error pages.

11.why: Passwords are stored only as bcrypt hashes, but the MFA secret '482913' is hardcoded directly in the source code.

12.why: No default username/password login exists and passwords must be user-set under a strong policy, but the fixed hardcoded MFA code acts like a shared default credential.

13.why: Per-session rate limiting throttles reset requests (3/15min), reset code guesses (5/15min), and MFA attempts (5/15min).

14.why: The reset-request endpoint returns the identical generic message and an opaque token for every valid-format email, revealing nothing about account existence.

15.why: Reset codes are 256-bit cryptographically random base64url strings, single-use, 15-minute expiry, and stored only for the specific session/account that requested them.
